author: Carlos Martinez
title: Monitor Stand vs. Triple Monitor Arm Setup for iRacing
description: Single-monitor stands offer simplicity and cost savings. Triple-monitor arms expand your field of view. Understand the real trade-offs to choose what fits your space and budget.

sections.p: When you sit down in a sim rig, your display setup shapes everything: how much peripheral vision you have, how much desk space gets consumed, how much money you spend, and how much time you spend installing or adjusting it. Most drivers begin with a single monitor on a basic stand. Some eventually move to three monitors on an articulated arm system. Neither approach is wrong. The difference comes down to your space, your budget, your current monitor setup, and what kind of racing you do most.
This guide breaks down what each setup actually offers, what the real friction points are, and how to think about which one makes sense for you right now.

A standard monitor stand is what it sounds like: a base that holds one screen at a fixed or adjustable angle, often with height and tilt controls. Most modern gaming monitors include one. If your monitor doesn't, you can buy a separate stand in the 20-50 dollar range, or use a wall mount or monitor arm designed for single displays.

The real appeal is simplicity. One cable run. One display to configure. One point of failure. The monitor sits at eye level, maybe slightly below, and you look straight ahead. For oval racing, this works fine. For road racing and street circuits, you lose the ability to see traffic or track detail off to the sides without moving your head, but many drivers manage this without real frustration.

list: Cost: $0 if your monitor already has a stand, $20-50 for a basic aftermarket stand
Space: minimal footprint. The stand takes up only a few inches of desk depth and width
Setup time: seconds. Just set the monitor on the stand and adjust the angle
Cable management: one main display cable plus power, easy to route
Field of view: ~45-50 degrees horizontal without head movement, enough for most oval and road racing at lower iRating
Vibration isolation: most basic stands do not dampen wheelbase or bass-shaker vibration effectively
Adjustment: monitor tilt and height, but fixed horizontal position

sections.tip: A single monitor at 1440p 120 Hz or higher pushes a strong GPU harder than two monitors, but not as hard as three. Frame consistency matters more than raw refresh rate for sim racing, so a smooth 80-100 Hz on one display often feels better than a stuttering 120 Hz.

sections.h2: Triple monitor on an arm setup

sections.p: A triple-monitor arm is an aluminum or steel articulated mount that holds three displays: one center and one on each side, typically angled outward in a gentle curve. Most common setups use three identical displays in landscape, roughly 24 to 27 inches each. The arm typically mounts to a desk or rig frame and offers adjustment for height, depth, rotation, and per-monitor tilt. Popular brands include Ergotron, North Bayou, and various generic equivalents available in the 150-400 dollar range depending on build quality and weight capacity.

The appeal is field of view. Three monitors give you roughly 130-150 degrees horizontal vision depending on bezel width and monitor size. In iRacing, this means you see track detail, traffic, and your own car's position in space without moving your head. On a street circuit or road course, this translates directly to confidence and lap time. You can pick an apex line, spot a competitor's front wing, and judge braking zones in real time.

list: Cost: $150-400 for the arm itself, plus three monitors (~$300-600 used, $600-1200 new) if you do not already own them
Space: 55-70 inches wide, 18-24 inches deep. This is a desk-mounted or rig-mounted sculpture that is visible and permanent
Setup time: 1-2 hours for initial mounting, cable routing, and angle tuning. Adjustment stays stable once dialed
Cable management: three display cables, three power cables, possibly USB. Routing behind a cockpit frame is tidier than on a desk
Field of view: 130-150 degrees without head movement, transforming spatial awareness in road racing
Vibration isolation: better isolation than a basic stand, especially with a rig frame mount; some arms flex slightly under high-torque wheelbase forces
Adjustment: independent tilt and height per monitor, plus overall arm rotation and depth for fine-tuning the curve

sections.tip: Three identical monitors are essential for symmetrical visuals. Mismatched sizes, resolutions, or refresh rates create disorienting depth cues and make the triple-screen presentation feel fractured.

sections.p: Here is where setup choice collides with hardware reality. A single 1440p 120 Hz monitor requires steady GPU output. Triple 1440p displays at the same refresh rate demand roughly 2.5x the pixel-pushing power. If your GPU is mid-range, you will hit a wall.

On an RTX 5060 Ti with a Ryzen 7 5700, running three 1440p 120 Hz monitors at high detail settings requires lowering resolution, refresh rate, or graphical fidelity. Most drivers running triple monitors reduce to 1080p per display or accept 60-80 Hz refresh to maintain smooth, consistent frame delivery. Some step down to two 1080p side monitors plus a 1440p center if they want to keep the GPU headroom for high settings.

A single monitor gives you more flexibility to chase higher fidelity or refresh rate without upgrading GPU. If you have a lower-tier GPU and want to maximize visual quality and frame consistency, a single monitor is the pragmatic choice.

olist: Estimate your GPU's sustained frame output at your target resolution and settings
Multiply by 2.5 for triple monitors to estimate the headroom needed
If that number is below your GPU's typical game throughput, you will need to compromise on resolution, refresh, or quality settings
Test with the monitors and settings you are considering before committing to the mount hardware

sections.p: A single monitor fits on any desk or rig frame. A triple-monitor arm is a different animal. It consumes 55-70 inches of width and projects forward. If your cockpit frame is a compact rig stand, the arm may overshoot the frame edges. If your desk is shared with a keyboard, mouse, or other gear, the monitors will dominate the real estate.

Mounting location matters. Rig-frame mount is cleaner and more stable than desk mount, but requires a rig that can accept the arm's bolt pattern. Desk mount is flexible but can introduce vibration transfer and look cluttered. Wall mount behind a rig frame is rigid and minimal but demands planning and often drywall anchors or studs.

If you are in an apartment or shared space, the visual and spatial footprint of a triple-monitor setup sends a signal. A single monitor looks like a gaming display. Three monitors look like a dedicated rig. If that is a conversation you want to have with roommates or family, plan accordingly.

A single monitor stand is a sunk cost of under 50 dollars. If you move to triple monitors later, you can sell the stand or repurpose it elsewhere. The monitors themselves hold value better if they are standard gaming units with broad compatibility.

A triple-monitor arm is a 150-400 dollar investment in a piece of hardware that works only for that specific purpose. If you later decide triple screens are not for you or you move and do not have space, the arm has limited resale value and limited other uses. The arm is a commitment.

Similarly, acquiring three monitors instead of one locks in a higher cost entry point. Used 1440p 144 Hz displays run $150-250 each, so three is $450-750. New ones are higher. A single monitor gets you started for $200-400. This matters if your budget is fixed.

sections.tip: If you are early in sim racing (Rookie or D-class), start with a single monitor. Learn racecraft and consistency first. Once you are confident you will stick with iRacing and you have the space and GPU headroom, triple monitors make tangible sense.

sections.p: The category of racing shapes the benefit equation. Oval racing relies on smooth steering input, throttle modulation, and line precision. Spatial awareness of traffic matters, but you are mostly working in the forward 30-45 degree cone. A single monitor works well. Many top oval racers use single screens.

Road racing and street circuits demand more spatial data. Spotting the apex of a 90-degree corner, judging braking distance on unfamiliar layouts, reading traffic three car-widths away. Triple monitors remove the guesswork. The peripheral vision transforms confidence and lap time, especially at tracks like Zandvoort, Laguna Seca, and Sebring where visibility and positioning matter.

If you race both, triple monitors favor road racing, but they do not penalize oval racing. You just get more visual real estate than you need. The overhead is the cost and space, not performance loss.

list: Start with a single monitor if you have limited space, budget under $500 total, own a mid-range GPU, or are new to sim racing
Consider triple monitors if you have 70+ inches of horizontal desk or rig space, a GPU with ~8GB VRAM, run mostly road racing, and are willing to invest $600-1200
Test borrowed triple-monitor setups at a friend's rig or at a sim racing community event before buying the arm and monitors
If you choose triple, plan the mount location and cable routing before purchase. Poor planning leads to frustration and often a partial setup that never gets finished
Monitor quality matters more than count. Three poor-quality displays create more problems than one good one. Buy used quality gear over new budget gear

faqs.q: Can I use different sized monitors in a triple setup?
faqs.a: Technically yes, but it is not recommended. Mismatched monitor sizes, resolutions, or refresh rates create disorienting perspective shifts and make the sim feel fractured. Identical 24-inch or 27-inch monitors at matching resolution and refresh rate (e.g., three 1440p 144Hz) are the standard. Identical secondhand monitors are often cheaper than one new high-end display.

faqs.q: Will a triple-monitor arm work on any desk?
faqs.a: Most articulated arms clamp or bolt to a desk edge or rig frame. Desk-mounted arms require at least 2-3 inches of clearance and a solid edge that can handle the weight (~15-30 lbs when loaded). Rig-frame mounting is more stable and looks cleaner but requires a frame with bolt holes or an adapter. Check the arm's clamping range and load rating before buying. Some arms do not fit thinner desks or modern narrow-edge designs.

faqs.q: How much GPU power do triple 1440p monitors really need?
faqs.a: Most drivers running three 1440p 120 Hz displays step down to 1080p per monitor or 60-80 Hz to maintain smooth frame delivery on mid-range GPUs. An RTX 5060 Ti can handle high-detail 1080p triple at 80-100 Hz or medium-detail 1440p triple at 60 Hz. If you want 1440p 120+ Hz on three monitors, you need a high-end GPU like an RTX 5080 or RTX 6900 XT. Test your specific settings and monitor configuration in iRacing before committing to the hardware.

faqs.q: Is there a middle ground between one and three monitors?
faqs.a: Yes. Some drivers use two 1440p displays: one centered 1440p high-refresh monitor plus two 1080p side monitors on a dual-arm mount. This gives better peripheral vision than single while reducing GPU load and cost versus a full triple setup. The bezel gap is more noticeable than on three identical displays, but the compromise appeals to drivers with limited space or GPU headroom. Dual-monitor arms are less common than single or triple, so finding them secondhand takes more patience.
